results.title: Falling Token Prices Hide Flat or Rising GPU Rents - Overfitted #53
highlights:
### Nvidia B200 spot rental rates have more than doubled since March, while barely 4.5% of US consumers pay anything for models.

...

The Decoder reports data from Ornn, Silicon Data and Bloomberg, as of August 2026, showing what a16z calls a textbook Jevons paradox in the AI market: token prices keep dropping, but H100 GPU rental prices hold steady or climb. The bullish logic, as the Decoder lays it out, is that cheaper tokens enable AI agents, automation and new applications, so volume grows faster than per-unit costs fall. It is a coherent argument. It is also a forecast about volume, presented as if it were a description of the present.

...

The first half of that claim is where the evidence is weakest. Token prices do fall, and that part holds. What the claim leaves out is the input side. The H100 rental price is flat or rising rather than falling alongside the token price. At the newer end of the product line the move is sharper: according to data from Ornn, a startup that maintains indexes, the hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March.

So the claim overshoots by the full distance between a falling price and a doubled one. At best, the cost of the hardware is flat. Anyone running the hardware is selling a cheaper unit while paying the same or more to produce it. That is a margin squeeze, and calling it deflation misdescribes it.

...

Now the supply side. SemiAnalysis counted 323 Nvidia GPU providers as of September, up from 209 less than 11 months earlier. That is a lot of new sellers of GPU time, and the rental data above shows rents holding or climbing rather than collapsing. More sellers have not yet produced cheaper hardware in the numbers we have. Whether that changes depends on whether the buyers keep showing up.

...

What the evidence does not show is that it is happening yet at a scale that covers the build-out. Only 4.5% of US consumers pay, the typical payer sits at about $25 a month, and the top 1% supplies a fifth of observed spending. The hardware market is moving the other way from the headline price, with H100 GPU rental prices holding steady or climbing and the hourly spot price for an Nvidia B200 GPU more than doubling since March, according to Ornn. The whole system rests on one assumption: AI usage has to grow fast enough to offset falling token prices.

results.title: Alexey Gubarev: Why Compute Stopped Getting Cheaper
highlights:
The numbers from the past few months all point the same way. Cushman & Wakefield's 2026 cost guide puts all-in greenfield development at $17.6 million per megawatt in the U.S. and Canada for the newest facilities, with land and power infrastructure included and chips and GPUs excluded. The building itself is only part of that: JLL puts shell-and-core construction at about $11.3 million per megawatt. The gap between the two numbers is land, grid connection, and electrical plant, and power infrastructure is now the largest single slice of the bill. CBRE reports that vacancy in North America's primary data center markets fell to a record 1.4% in the first half of the year, while asking rents rose by between 4.3% and 8.3%, depending on deployment size. Memory has joined in: TrendForce expects server DRAM contract prices to rise another 13–18% in the third quarter. For operators, there is an opportunity in all this. When capacity is this scarce, whoever can hand over a working megawatt on schedule can charge for it, and customers will sign long contracts to be sure of getting it.

...

Today a GPU is one component of what a customer really pays for. The rest is a powered, cooled, and connected rack, and each of those inputs has its own supply problem. Satya Nadella put it plainly on the BG2 podcast last November: "It's not a supply issue of chips; it's the fact that I don't have warm shells to plug into." If the head of Microsoft says the building is the constraint, the building is going to set the price.

## What GPU rental prices are really saying

At first glance, rental rates look like a counter-argument. According to the price tracker Silicon Data, H100 rates fell from around $8 an hour in early 2024 to between $1.50 and $3.00 by late 2025. Look more closely, though. The fall has stopped: Silicon Data's H100 index jumped 10% between early December and early January, its biggest short-term move since mid-2025.

And the same chip rents for roughly $1.90 an hour from specialist providers and more than $4 from the largest clouds. A twofold spread on identical silicon means customers aren't paying for the chip. They're paying for guaranteed capacity, in a building with power, close to the rest of their systems.

...

They get more work out of what is already installed. That means better scheduling, keeping older GPUs in service for inference and moving jobs to wherever capacity is free that week. It's unglamorous. It's also where margin comes from when hardware alone no longer delivers it.

results.title: Nvidia GPUs become core AI resource as firms mobilise all channels to secure supply
highlights:
Nvidia graphics processing units have become a key resource for AI infrastructure, pushing companies to change how they procure computing capacity. Firms are expanding beyond reliance on large cloud providers such as AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, using neocloud specialists, online marketplaces, direct equipment purchases and customer-supplied hardware models. Demand continues to outstrip supply, and providers and customers are multiplying even as prices rise and prepayments and long-term contracts add to procurement costs.

...

As Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) become a core resource for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, companies are rapidly changing how they procure them. Firms that relied on large cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are moving to secure compute capacity by also using neoclouds, online marketplaces and direct purchases of their own equipment.

CNBC reported on Oct. 10 that as AI computing demand continues to outstrip supply, companies are using multiple channels at the same time to secure GPUs. With supply shortages and rising prices overlapping, a broader push is spreading to diversify procurement sources rather than rely on a single provider.

Rising demand is also reflected in Nvidia's earnings outlook. Nvidia set quarterly revenue guidance for the October quarter at $108 billion. That is up 89 percent from a year earlier. As demand for AI infrastructure rises, the number of providers supplying GPUs has also increased rapidly. Market research firm SemiAnalysis counted 323 providers offering Nvidia GPUs as of September. That was a sharp increase from 209 less than 11 months earlier.

...

But big cloud providers alone are finding it harder to handle surging demand. Gartner's Hardip Singh (하딥 싱) said large providers can give trust to enterprise customers, but do not always have as many GPUs as needed. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy (앤디 재시) also said it will be difficult to handle all expected demand this year and that supply shortages could continue until 2027.

Neoclouds are filling that gap. Neoclouds are specialist cloud providers that offer services centred on GPUs and AI computing resources. With more flexible contract terms and more granular supply methods than large cloud providers, they are emerging as an alternative for AI companies.

...

Neoclouds' strength lies in flexibility of supply and contracts. Some providers offer GPUs in relatively small units without prepayment or long-term contracts. But the more demand concentrates on a provider, the more it may require prepayment or take months before GPUs are actually up and running.

CoreWeave Vice President Chen Goldberg (첸 골드버그) said it is not possible to provide 10,000 GPUs to a new customer in a single day. CEO Mike Intrator (마이크 인트레이터) also said short-term GPU supply capacity is effectively sold out. That means neoclouds are emerging as an alternative, but they too are not free from shortages.

...

Moves are also emerging to secure large GPU capacity through long-term contracts. SpaceX agreed to provide GPU capacity to Google and Reflection, and in May it signed a GPU rental contract worth $1.25 billion per month with Anthropic through mid-2029. SpaceX Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen (브렛 존슨) said the current economics have reduced the payback period for investment in new computing facilities to less than 1 year.

...

The problem is that GPU prices are also rising rapidly. Data compiled by Orion shows the hourly spot price of an Nvidia B200 GPU has more than doubled since March. The channels to obtain GPUs are diversifying, but supply shortages, rising prices and the burden of prepayments and long-term contracts remain factors that raise procurement costs for companies.

results.title: How expensive is US AI compute rental? "Spot prices" are 2x long-term contracts and 4x cloud providers' return threshold | PANews English
highlights:
The US AI compute rental market is showing a clear "short-term expensive, long-term cheap" pattern.

On October 10, according to a chart in Goldman Sachs internet analyst Eric Sheridan's SpaceX quarterly preview report, the annualized revenue for one gigawatt of compute is roughly $40 billion to $50 billion for short-term spot rentals, roughly $20 billion to $30 billion for long-term contracts, while the breakeven threshold for hyperscalers' self-built capacity is only about $12 billion.

But Goldman Sachs' analysis holds that the fundamental reason hyperscalers like Google rent compute at a steep premium is that their self-built capacity cannot keep up; once self-built capacity catches up, the spot premium will disappear. It forecasts that SpaceX alone will grow its compute scale from 1.4 gigawatts in Q2 2026 to roughly 7 gigawatts by the end of 2027 and roughly 10.6 gigawatts by the end of 2028 — a more than 7x expansion in four years. Compute supply across the entire industry is increasing rapidly.

...

The Goldman Sachs report shows that SpaceX announced two new compute colocation contracts over the past quarter and told investors these contracts were "priced at the high end of the historically discussed range of $30 billion to $50 billion per gigawatt."

SpaceX is not an isolated case.

- Nebius (NBIS) disclosed in August that its third-quarter short-term compute contract pricing was roughly $40 billion to $50 billion per gigawatt.
- CoreWeave (CRWV) disclosed that recent short-term contract pricing was roughly $40 billion per gigawatt.
- IREN disclosed that recent three-year contract pricing exceeded $20 billion per gigawatt, with contracts under negotiation at roughly $25 billion per gigawatt.
- Nebius long-term contract pricing was likewise in the $20 billion to $25 billion per gigawatt range.

Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu, in his "Got compute?" report, further broke down the GPU-hour pricing of SpaceX's individual contracts, concluding that the Google and Reflection AI contracts were roughly $50 million to $51 million per megawatt, while two other undisclosed customers were roughly $60 million to $61 million per megawatt — which converts to as much as $61 billion per gigawatt, with GB300 chip hourly rental approaching $14.

...

Short-term spot prices are roughly twice long-term contract prices. The lower bound of long-term agreement pricing currently remains at about $20 billion per GW.

This inverted term structure has a specific name in commodity markets: backwardation. It usually means the market views the current shortage as a temporary phenomenon.

In other words, buyers are willing to pay a premium for "no commitment," which precisely shows that while demand is real, even the buyers themselves are unsure whether this demand can last.

...

Current short-term hyperscaler cloud rents are 2 to 4 times this threshold.

What does this mean?

Google rents SpaceX compute at roughly $45 billion per gigawatt (Deutsche Bank estimates $50 billion), while Goldman Sachs' ROIC framework shows that Google's self-built data centers need only about $12 billion per gigawatt in returns.

No one pays a 4x premium for a commodity unless they have no alternative. The analysis points out that Google rents compute because its self-build speed cannot keep up. Once self-built capacity catches up, the rental premium will disappear, and hyperscaler cloud revenue will shrink sharply along with it.

...

results.title: Why Neoclouds Are Adding a Second Demand Channel | packet.ai
highlights:
Supply is booming. Demand is lumpy. That is the neocloud business model problem, and it is why the neocloud demand channel mix is changing, as a growing number of GPU clouds pair direct sales with a second demand channel (a compute marketplace that sells capacity to many smaller buyers), though the evidence is a pattern across examples, not a census. This piece sets out the evidence in public filings and independent research, then says what we think follows from it. Every market claim is sourced and dated, and our own opinions are marked "Our view." One disclosure up front: packet.ai runs a provider program that lets operators list capacity on a B2B marketplace, so we have a stake in this argument and you should weigh it accordingly.

...

- The long tail of GPU clouds keeps growing: SemiAnalysis tracked 209 providers in November 2025, up from 124 a year earlier, yet the 84 it rated covered 95% of the market by volume
- Demand at the top is large and concentrated: CoreWeave reported $60.7 billion of remaining performance obligations at the end of 2025, with Microsoft about 67% of 2025 revenue, and says its backlog should grow in steps, with possible periods of decline
- The biggest deals rest on credit support a small operator does not have: Google backstopped specific Fluidstack lease obligations that support project debt, $1.8 billion at TeraWulf's Lake Mariner and about $1.3 billion at a later 168 MW joint venture at its Abernathy campus
- Sacra estimates that at the end of 2024 about 62% of Fluidstack's revenue came from private cloud and about 38% from its marketplace, with average contracts of over $100 million against about $340,000
- Our view: a marketplace adds many small buyers and short terms but typically not the long, predictable contracts that support financing, and the main risk, channel conflict, is manageable with separate inventory and clear pricing rules

...

Start with supply. SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX 2.0 (November 2025) tracked 209 GPU cloud providers, up from 169 in March 2025 and 124 a year before. It rated 84 of them and said those 84 cover 95% of the market by volume. By simple arithmetic that leaves the other 125 or so tracked providers sharing roughly 5%, which is what a long tail looks like.

AI compute demand at the top is large but concentrated. CoreWeave's FY2025 10-K reports $60.7 billion of remaining performance obligations at December 31, 2025, up from $15.1 billion a year earlier, and says Microsoft accounted for about 67% of its 2025 revenue. It also discloses commitments of up to about $11.9 billion from OpenAI through October 2030 and up to about $14.2 billion from Meta through December 2031. The same filing says the company expects backlog to grow "in steps, which may include periods of decline," and expects customer concentration to continue.

None of this means the gpu rental market is slack. SemiAnalysis's April 2026 analysis, titled "The Great GPU Shortage," reported its H100 one-year contract price index up almost 40% between October 2025 and March 2026, a measure of one GPU model on one contract length and not of every provider. Capacity can be tight for the largest buyers and thin for everyone else at the same time. A growing market is also not the same as a growing set of buyers that any one provider can reach: the totals describe aggregate demand, not the demand an individual operator can win.

...

The tightness is real at the top, where a few large buyers sign multi-year commitments with a handful of providers. Operators outside that group tend to see demand arrive in lumps: a customer takes a block of capacity, leaves, and the hours in between sit idle. That is an inference from the evidence above, not a measured statistic.

The chain of reasoning, in four steps (our view):

1. Large buyers sign long contracts that support financing and capacity planning.
2. Those buyers cannot absorb every GPU, configuration or time window a provider has.
3. Smaller buyers can supply incremental demand, usually on shorter commitments.
4. The provider gains another route to sell capacity, but takes on pricing and customer-overlap risk that has to be managed.

results.title: GPU Futures: How Compute Is Becoming an Exchange-Traded Commodity – Buzko Legal
highlights:
CME Group’s New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) is getting ready to list the first futures on AI compute rental prices ever to trade on a regulated U.S. exchange. Each contract covers one month of rental time on a single Nvidia H100 or B200 GPU. Trading was originally set to begin on October 5, 2026, but on September 21, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) extended its review of the contracts until November 9.

...

The basic unit in this market is the GPU-hour, which is one GPU (an Nvidia H100, for example) working for a customer for one hour. In practice, GPUs are rented in nodes of eight and in clusters of hundreds of nodes rather than one at a time, but prices are still quoted per GPU-hour. For simplicity we call this “rental,” although, as the second article showed, these deals are more often structured as compute services than as equipment leases.

...

There is no fixed conversion rate between the two. Depending on the provider, a node of eight H100s rents for anywhere from $15 to $100 an hour. One provider can squeeze tens of millions of tokens an hour out of it, while another, running weaker software, gets only a fraction of that. Both layers have their own indexes, and both index providers we discuss below publish prices for GPU-hours as well as tokens. This article focuses on GPU-hours.

...

Later on, we show how an exchange decouples price protection from that risk.

...

Take one hour on an Nvidia H100, the workhorse chip of the AI boom, on October 5, 2026, the day the CME futures were originally supposed to start trading. The hyperscalers are the most expensive. Azure charges $12.29, Google Cloud $11.06, and AWS $6.88. These per-GPU figures are our own calculations. All three sell their flagship H100 setups as eight-GPU nodes, so we divided the node price (for Azure, $98.32 an hour) by eight.

Neoclouds are cheaper. CoreWeave lists the H100 at $6.16, Lambda at $3.99, and Nebius at $4.50. These are sticker prices too, the starting point for negotiations.

The indexes we cover below are lower still. Silicon Data’s neocloud index stands at $2.81, and Ornn’s index of executed trades is at $2.52. The gap between a neocloud’s list price and the index is exactly the discount you will not find in public sources.

...

## The same H100 rents for anywhere from $1.79 to $12.29 an hour

What it cost to rent one Nvidia H100 GPU for an hour on October 5, 2026. Hyperscaler prices are the eight-GPU node price divided by eight. Index data from Silicon Data and Ornn.

| Provider or index | Segment | What it measures | $ per GPU-hour |

| Microsoft Azure | Hyperscalers | ND96isr H100 v5 node, $98.32 for 8 GPUs | 12,29 |
| Google Cloud | Hyperscalers | a3-highgpu-8g node, $88.49 for 8 GPUs | 11,06 |
| Silicon Data index | Hyperscalers | hyperscalers, on-demand | 7,16 |
| AWS | Hyperscalers | p5.48xlarge node, $55.04 for 8 GPUs | 6,88 |

...

On top of that, a GPU-hour has two quirks that no traditional commodity shares:

1. It cannot be stored. An unused hour is gone forever, like an empty seat on a plane. You cannot buy hours cheaply today, warehouse them, and sell them a year later.
2. Chips go obsolete. Nvidia ships a new generation every 12–18 months (the A100, H100, H200, B200, and B300, with Vera Rubin arriving in 2026), and each new generation pushes the previous one down the price ladder. A three-year H100 contract will outlast two of them.

All this makes prices volatile. At the height of the 2023–2024 shortage, an H100 cost $7–10 an hour. By 2025, supply had caught up with demand. AWS cut prices on its H100 instances by 44% in a single announcement, and according to Silicon Data, neocloud H100 rates fell 45% between September 2024 and February 2025. In 2026, prices reversed course. According to the SemiAnalysis index, one-year H100 rates climbed from $1.70 in October 2025 to $2.35 in March 2026, up almost 40%, as inference and agentic workloads soaked up capacity faster than new data centers could come online. Neocloud list prices are going up too. On October 1, 2026, Nebius raised its on-demand prices for the second time in three months, lifting the H100 by about 17%.

results.title: Falling AI Token Prices Are Fuelling Higher Nvidia GPU Demand — Renascence
highlights:
New a16z analysis shows Nvidia H100 rental rates holding steady despite falling AI token prices, a Jevons paradox effect that matches Jensen Huang's demand forecast.

...

New analysis from venture firm a16z highlights a Jevons paradox playing out in the AI infrastructure market: even as the price of AI tokens keeps falling, rental rates for Nvidia H100 GPUs are holding steady or edging higher. Rather than cheaper inference costs shrinking demand for compute, they appear to be accelerating it, as falling token prices make AI applications viable for a wider range of use cases.

The dynamic matters because it is the scenario Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has consistently pointed to as the industry's best-case trajectory: that efficiency gains in running AI models do not cannibalise demand for the underlying hardware, but instead expand the pool of workloads that make economic sense to run, keeping pressure on GPU supply.

The Decoder's reporting frames this as a fragile equilibrium. The entire chain — from chip manufacturers through cloud providers to AI application builders — is currently calibrated on the assumption that falling per-token costs will keep unlocking new demand faster than costs decline. If that demand growth were to plateau, the knock-on effects would be felt across the stack, from GPU rental pricing to the capital expenditure plans of cloud and AI infrastructure providers.

results.title: Short-Term AI Compute Contracts Price Near Double Long-Term Deals | TokenPost
highlights:
Short-term AI-compute contracts are priced at roughly twice the level of longer agreements, highlighting the premium for immediate capacity as companies expand power, facilities and GPU availability.

Nebius disclosed Aug. 12, 2026, that short-duration capacity was priced at approximately $40 million to $50 million per megawatt of annualized revenue. That equals $40 billion to $50 billion per gigawatt annually. These arrangements typically cover periods ranging from three to six months.

Longer-term agreements were priced at approximately $20 million to $25 million per megawatt annually, or $20 billion to $25 billion per gigawatt. The lower pricing provides suppliers with more predictable revenue and can support financing for expansion.

Nebius also indicated that it could sell its entire 2027 capacity at the short-term pricing level. The comparison shows how customers seeking immediate access to constrained infrastructure may pay more than those committing to longer arrangements.

...

A Google Cloud Services Agreement signed June 5, 2026, covers approximately 110,000 NVIDIA GPUs. The agreement calls for payments of $920 million per month from October 2026 through June 2029.

After Dec. 31, 2026, either side can end the agreement by providing 90 days' notice. That provision means the stated payment schedule does not necessarily guarantee revenue through the full term.

The pricing gap underscores the trade-off between urgency and commitment in AI infrastructure. Shorter contracts can command higher annualized pricing when capacity is scarce, while longer agreements can provide the revenue visibility needed to finance new capacity. Expansion by major AI-compute buyers will determine how much pressure develops on the premium.
